word_order: SVO | Samples show canonical subject–verb–object ordering (e.g. 'Steve Jobs unveiled the device', 'Mutations can have a variety of different effects').
register: Edited written prose: mainly formal news/encyclopedic/technical prose (news reports, encyclopedia-style descriptions, and technical notes).
clause_boundary_signals: subordinating conjunctions that introduce dependent clauses (although, because)
coordinating conjunctions that join clauses (and, but)
relative/complementizer pronouns that embed clauses (that, which)
non_boundary_traps: long prepositional modifiers and prepositional openings that look clause-like (for over a thousand years, of the Apollo X command module)
appositive or parenthetical noun phrases and title phrases (Wladyslaw Gomulka as the new prime minister, Sir Richard Branson's Virgin Group)
quantifier phrases and numeral phrases that begin a clause but continue the NP (eighteen percent of Venezuelans, around 60 cases)
unstable_prefix_signals: subordinating/conditional opens whose interpretation depends on the following clause (if, although)
focus/quantifier fronting that can take different scopes depending on continuation (only, most)
notes_for_prompt_writer: English in these samples is SVO and uses a rich set of clause-linking words (subordinators, coordinators, relative/complementizer pronouns). Noun phrases are frequently long and can contain embedded modifiers (prepositional phrases, appositives, relative clauses) that are not independent clauses. Many discourse markers are multi-word (e.g., 'of course', 'in reality'), and focus/quantifier items (e.g., 'only', 'most') can change interpretation depending on following material.
